I read the paper, there is a pretty interesting nuance missed by this news article.

The negative comments examined were not specifically directed towards the player. Instead, they simply coded everything said by any player in teamspeak, regardless of who they were talking to. In other words, male gamers who perform poorly express themselves more negatively in the presence of women, as opposed to expressing themselves negatively towards women.

This difference completely changes the way to interpret the results. Are male gamers who perform poorly more "sexist"? We have no idea. Are male gamers who perform poorly more likely to try to compensate for their performance in front of a female audience than in front of a male audience? Probably.

Charlie is an excelent dog, but the one area he lacks in is his behavior with other dogs. He makes really quick movements, muzzle punches, and barks and growls a lot. its awful. Its scary and it freaks the other dog owners out and most of the time starts a fight. He isnt being aggressive, which others find hard to believe, because if the other dog can ignore his awful noises, they can play together. I even have a video of him playing with my moms Shih-tzu poodle mix puppy.

Currently, he isnt allowed to go to the dog park, per my request, so he doesnt get hurt or hurt anybody else. He is really sad and i want him to be able to go to the dog park and have fun, but cant seem to figure out how to help him! Here are all the things I have tried and am currently trying.

-We have completed his leash training, and he is now currently learning to walk beside/behind me. -We are now learning to sit and be calm when entering a park or going outside. (which is hard because I am not 100% sure he understands pack mentality) -I had a thought to try lying him on his back to help show him how to be more submissive to the other dogs. -We have eliminated the use of toys in the park, because i feel that once he gets a tennis ball, his mind goes out the window. -We are staring to get him used to the bike, so maybe we can bike with him to help expend some of his energy. -We were going to try giving him a backpack on walks, an idea i saw on Cesar 911, to give him a job and keep him satisfied.

We have tried so many things that i probably can't list. He doesnt seem to understand being dominant/submissive, or even alpha/beta/omega. The shelter staff seemed to think he was just tied up outside and forgotten about, so there is little to no socialization present, and I cant seem to help him.

I just want what is best for Charlie, and to help him be the best dog he can. PLEASE help us. :(

Caytie and Charlie
Clueless Dog seeks help making friends

Hi Caytie!

He doesnt seem to understand being dominant/submissive, or even alpha/beta/omega.

Dogs do not form social hierarchies with an alpha, which is why your dog wouldn't understand this concept. Many years ago, it was thought that dogs were constantly fighting to be higher rank and that this was the cause of behavioral problems, but modern research has revealed that the original theory (referred to as "dominance theory") didn't apply to wolves, much less to dogs which are so far removed. You can read more on this here, here, and here. Knowing this, it does absolutely nothing to roll your dog onto their back (other than maybe annoy them slightly).

On to the issue: often dogs behave this way because they didn't learn appropriate play as puppies. Normally when puppies play, they get growled or nipped for being too rough and so they learn what is ok to do and what isn't early on. I definitely agree with the shelter that they likely weren't socialized much and as a result they simply never learned this concept.

In cases like this, it's difficult to teach the dog appropriate play without another dog that can clearly communicate when the play has gone too far without initiating a fight. I'd really encourage you to find a trainer who has experience in this area. However, if you'd really like to give it a try yourself, you can:

Get a really long leash (or string several leashes together) and attach it to a harness on your dog. Allow your dog to play and the second the play gets too rough (snarling, biting, the other dog is visibly annoyed), pull your dog in and give them a short time out. After some time, release them to play again and repeat until they learn that if they play too roughly, they don't get to play. This may take some time, especially if you don't have another dog that's good at teaching manners, but eventually they get the idea. In some cases, especially with an older dog, it really does take a special kind of playmate to help them understand what kind of play is appropriate. This is a common issue and many, many trainers have dogs on hand just for such an occasion - ask around. :)

Do you have a trainer who organizes dog playgroups or socials? My trainer has "doggy socials" that are all entirely structured and very good for dogs with behavioral problems, particularly if they weren't socialized enough as a puppy. Or if you have a trainer who can observe his behavior with other dogs and help you moderate and teach as needed. A dog park is one of the worst places for a dog to be, regardless of behavior or manners, and I don't take my dog to a dog park at all. Also he shouldn't have toys, food, or other things that can trigger aggression if he's around other dogs. Set him up for success as much as possible but be ready to guide him when he needs it.

Rolling your dog on his back to "show submission" doesn't do anything besides instill fear or annoyance in your dog. Dominance theory is outdated and pack mentality in dogs is very fluid. I would also possibly look into group obedience classes (stay away from anything taught at Petsmart or Petco or other large chain stores) to teach him to focus on you when he's around other dogs and to work on teaching appropriate obedience skills. Really, I would recommend working with a trainer in this case so they can read the dog's behavior and body language and teach you appropriate methods to reel him in as needed.
